power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Purpose.

The short UPPS-P (SUPPS-P) is a widely used, gold-standard measure capturing five facets of impulsivity, including negative urgency, (lack of) premeditation, (lack of) perseverance, sensation seeking, and positive urgency.

However, most validation studies have been conducted in relatively small convenience samples, few utilize multi-wave data, and no formal psychometric evaluation of the SUPPS-P has been conducted in a Danish sample.
Procedures.

Up to 2,745 adolescents (65.46% female, Mage=16.77 [SD=0.58] at baseline) completed the Danish SUPPS-P, as well as measures of substance use, self-efficacy, wellbeing, and internalizing symptoms at four timepoints over a 12-month period.
Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to evaluate fit of the established SUPPS-P five-factor structure and test measurement invariance across biological sex.
Convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity; internal consistency; and test-retest reliability were evaluated for each subscale.
Main Findings.
Replicating past studies, a five-factor model best fit the data, but several items loaded weakly on the lack of perseverance and sensation seeking factors.
Measurement invariance across biological sex was established.

Positive correlations with substance use, negative correlations with self-efficacy and well-being, and subscale-specific correlations with internalizing symptoms supported convergent and discriminant validity.
Correlations of baseline SUPPS-P scores with external variables up to 12 months later supported predictive validity.
Internal consistency was acceptable for all subscales (ω=0.67-0.81) and moderate intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC=0.51-0.69) supported adequate testretest reliability.
Conclusions.
The SUPPS-P is suitable for assessing impulsivity in Danish adolescents over time, though further research is needed to optimize the measure's psychometric properties in this group.

Impulsivity reflects a tendency to "overlook important information prior to making a decision, take unreasonably high risks, and opt for immediate rather than delayed payoffs in intertemporal choices" [1] and is related to a wide range of psychiatric conditions and health risk behaviors, including substance use [2].

text.text: >Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: Data were drawn from a parent substance use intervention study in Danish high school students [35, 38].
text.formatted: Data were drawn from a parent substance use intervention study in Danish high school students <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">38]</ref>.

text.text: The original trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID NCT06018389) and the Danish Data Protection Agency.
Institutional review board (IRB) approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee at Aarhus University, Denmark (ID BSS-2023-039).
In spring 2023, 64 public high schools were invited to participate in the study via email.
Sixteen schools from 13 Danish cities agreed to participate.
Eligibility criteria for students included being an incoming first-year student in August 2023, at least 15 years of age, and able to understand and speak Danish.
As the age of consent for research participation in Denmark is 15, students were able to independently consent to participation.
Students and their parents/guardians received written information about the study at least one week before the study team visited campuses to conduct enrollment procedures.
Information included that participation was voluntary and that students had the right to withdraw at any time.
Consent was provided ahead of survey administration.
Surveys were completed on-site in schools during class periods at five waves (baseline, 2-, 6-, 9-, and 12-months) with members of the research team present at each survey administration.
The present study included 2,745 students who provided SUPPS-P data at baseline and participated in at least one of the follow-ups.
The English version of the 20-item SUPPS-P [8] was used as the basis for translation to Danish.
text.formatted: The English version of the 20-item SUPPS-P <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8]</ref> was used as the basis for translation to Danish.

text.text: Two native Danish speakers fluent in English independently translated all items into Danish, discussed the translations, and came to agreement.
Danish items were then backtranslated by a native English and Danish speaker.
Two senior team members then finalized the translation.
The final version of the Danish SUPPS-P is available upon request.
Items were rated on a 1 (agree strongly) to 4 (disagree strongly) scale and mean scores were calculated for each subscale.
Where indicated, items were recoded such that higher scores reflect higher impulsivity.
The Danish SUPPS-P was administered at baseline and 6-, 9-, and 12-month follow-ups.
Frequency of intoxication in the past 30 days was assessed via a single item querying "How many times how you gotten drunk from drinking alcohol within the past 30 days?"
Respondents could select options ranging from 0-30.
Students who reported no alcohol use in the past 30 days were coded as having 0 drunk days.

Number of binge drinking days, maximum drinks per drinking occasion, and total drinks in the past 30 days were assessed using the Timeline Follow-Back (TLFB) (32), a calendar-based assessment that prompts recall of substance use patterns by referencing dates, weekends, and notable events (e.g., semester start or holidays).
text.formatted: Number of binge drinking days, maximum drinks per drinking occasion, and total drinks in the past 30 days were assessed using the Timeline Follow-Back (TLFB) <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(32)</ref>, a calendar-based assessment that prompts recall of substance use patterns by referencing dates, weekends, and notable events (e.g., semester start or holidays).

text.text: The TLFB is the gold standard for assessing quantity and frequency of substance use in the adolescent age group, with the computer-based version demonstrating comparable reliability to interview-based formats [39, 40].
text.formatted: The TLFB is the gold standard for assessing quantity and frequency of substance use in the adolescent age group, with the computer-based version demonstrating comparable reliability to interview-based formats <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">40]</ref>.

text.text: Among students who endorsed past 30 day nicotine use, frequency of smoking cigarettes and frequency of vaping in the past 30 days were assessed via single items querying "Think about the last 30 days.
How many days have you: smoked cigarettes?"
and "Think about the last 30 days.
How many days have you: used e-cigarettes/vape/puff bars?"
Respondents could select options ranging from 1-30.
Students who did not endorse nicotine use in the past 30 days were coded as having 0 use days.
Self-efficacy was measured via three items from the World Health Organization Health
Behavior in School-age Children survey.

Questions included "How often can you find a solution to problems if you try hard enough?", "How often can you achieve what you set your mind to?", and "How often do you succeed in learning what you want at school?"
Items were rated on a 1 (always) to 5 (never) scale.
Items were reverse coded such that higher scores reflect higher self-efficacy, and a mean score was subsequently derived from the three items.

Mental well-being was measured via the World Health Organization Well-Being Index, a 5-item measure assessing frequency of feeling cheerful and in good spirits, calm and relaxed, active and vigorous, refreshed and rested after waking, and as though daily life has been filled with things of interest over the past two weeks.
Items were rated on a 0 (at no time) to 5 (all the time) scale and summed to create a total score.
Internalizing (depression and anxiety) symptoms were measured via the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-4, a 4-item measure consisting of a 2-item depression scale and a 2-item anxiety scale [41].
text.formatted: Internalizing (depression and anxiety) symptoms were measured via the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-4, a 4-item measure consisting of a 2-item depression scale and a 2-item anxiety scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Frequency of symptoms over the past two weeks are rated on a 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day) scale.
Items were summed to create a total symptom score.
Analyses were conducted using SAS 9.4 [42] and Mplus version 9 [43].
text.formatted: Analyses were conducted using SAS 9.4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[42]</ref> and Mplus version 9 <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[43]</ref>.

text.text: Inter-item correlations for all 20 SUPPS-P items and item-total correlations within each SUPPS-P subscale were estimated using baseline data.

To examine whether the established factor structure of the SUPPS-P replicates in this sample of Danish adolescents, four confirmatory factor models were fit using data from the baseline measurement occasion.

This sequence of models mirrored that in the English SUPPS-P validation study [8]: 1) a one-factor model, wherein all 20 SUPPS-P items load onto a single "impulsivity" factor, 2) a five-factor model, with one factor corresponding to each subscale and freely estimated intercorrelations between factors, 3) a higher-order five-factor model, with one factor corresponding to each subscale and a higher-order "impulsivity" factor, and 4) a three-factor hierarchical model, with negative and positive urgency as lower-order factors subsumed under a higher-order "emotion-based rash action" factor and lack of perseverance and premeditation as lower-order factors subsumed under a higher-order "deficits in conscientiousness" factor.

text.text: As the SUPPS-P items are measured on an ordinal scale, all models were estimated using weighted least squared mean variance (WLSMV) with robust standard errors to account for clustering within schools.

Evaluation of model fit was based on the comparative fit index (CFI) [44], the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) [45], the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) [46], and the root meansquare error of approximation (RMSEA) [47].

text.text: Configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance across biological sex were evaluated within the best-fit factor model.
Configural invariance tests whether the factor structure holds across groups and imposes no equality constraints on parameters.
Fit of the configural model was evaluated by the same criteria as the confirmatory models described above.

Metric invariance tests whether factor loadings are equal across groups by constraining loadings to equality across groups and evaluating deterioration in model fit compared to the unconstrained configural model.
Scalar invariance tests whether factor means are equal across groups by further adding equality constraints to item intercepts and evaluating deterioration in model fit compared to the metric model.

Strict invariance tests whether residual variances are equal across groups by further adding equality constraints to residual variances and evaluating deterioration in model fit compared to the scalar model.

Comparison of these nested models was conducted using the difftest function within Mplus, which performs a corrected  2 difference test that is appropriate for application to models for which the reported  2 is mean and variance adjusted.

Due to the corrected  2 test's sensitivity to sample size, additional criteria of Δ CFI of ≤0.010, Δ TLI of ≤0.010 (where a decrease beyond this threshold would suggest deterioration of fit), Δ SRMR of ≥0.030, and Δ RMSEA of ≥0.015 (where an increase beyond this threshold would suggest deterioration of model fit) were used as the primary metrics by which to compare models [16, [52] [53] [54].

text.text: Unpaired t-tests were used to evaluate mean differences of each subscale across males and females at each timepoint.

Spearman rank correlations between SUPPS-P subscales and external correlates (substance use, self-efficacy, mental well-being, internalizing symptoms) were estimated using baseline data to evaluate convergent and discriminant validity.

Predictive validity was evaluated by examining correlations between the SUPPS-P subscales at baseline and substance use, self-efficacy, mental well-being, and internalizing symptoms at 6-, 9-, and 12-month follow-ups.
Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω were calculated to evaluate internal consistency of each SUPPS-P subscale at each measurement occasion.

Test-retest reliability was evaluated via intraclass correlations (ICCs) between SUPPS-P subscale scores across all measurement occasions, as well as pairwise ICCs for baseline and each follow-up occasion.
ICCs were estimated using multinomial mixed effect models with random intercepts to account for repeated measures within students and school-level clustering.
Evaluation of test-retest reliability was based on established thresholds for ICCs wherein <0.50 is poor, 0.50-0.75 is moderate, 0.75-0.90 is good, and >0.90 is excellent [55].

text.text: As anticipated, SUPPS-P subscales at baseline were significantly, positively correlated with quantity and frequency of alcohol use, frequency of cigarette smoking, and frequency of vaping at both baseline (ρ=0.05-0.21) and, with the exception of lack of perseverance and alcohol use (ρ=0.03-.04, ns), at all timepoints through 12-month follow-up (ρ=0.05-0.16).

All subscales at baseline, except sensation seeking (ρ=.18-.20), were significantly, negatively correlated with self-efficacy and mental well-being at baseline (ρ=-0.04--0.36) and at all timepoints through 12month follow-up (ρ=-0.04--0.27).

Negative urgency, lack of premeditation, and positive urgency at baseline were positively correlated with internalizing symptoms at baseline (ρ=0.07-0.25) and, with the exception of positive urgency (ρ=.03, ns), at all timepoints through 12-month follow-up.

Sensation seeking was significantly negatively correlated with internalizing symptoms at all timepoints (ρ=-0.13--.17) and, in contrast to past studies, lack of perseverance was uncorrelated at all timepoints (ρ=-0.02-.01, ns).

text.text: Both Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω are reported per convention, although internal consistencies were evaluated primarily using McDonald's ω as it does not assume tau equivalence across items and is more appropriate for use with items measured on an ordinal scale.
All subscales demonstrated acceptable reliability at baseline (ω=0.73-0.81), except lack of perseverance (ω=0.67).
Reliabilities for all subscales met or exceeded acceptable thresholds at 6-month follow-up (ω=0.72-0.83), 9-month follow-up (ω=0.75-0.85), and 12-month follow-up (ω=0.73-0.88).
Test-retest reliability was evaluated via ICCs for each SUPPS-P subscale, captured by both an overall ICC across timepoints and pairwise ICCs between baseline and each follow-up.
Overall ICCs indicated moderate reliability for all scales (ICC=0.51-0.69).

Pairwise ICCs between baseline and each follow-up similarly showed moderate reliability for negative urgency (ICC=0.48-0.51), lack of premeditation (ICC=0.55-0.61), sensation seeking (ICC=0.65-0.66), and positive urgency (ICC=0.52-0.57); lack of perseverance again showed borderline poor reliability (ICC=0.46-0.48).
As expected, ICCs showed small decreases at more distal timepoints.

To our knowledge, this is one of the most comprehensive validation studies of the Short UPPS-P Impulsive Behavior Scale in an adolescent sample, and the first to validate the Danish version of SUPPS-P. This study was strengthened by the large sample size and multi-wave design, permitting robust estimation and evaluation of psychometric properties of the SUPPS-P over time.

In line with a large literature on translations of the SUPPS-P [8, 12, 16, 19-21, 23-26, 28, 31], the data supported a five-factor structure with established measurement invariance across biological sex.

text.text: Patterns of correlation with substance use, self-efficacy, mental wellbeing, and internalizing symptoms supported convergent and discriminant validity.
Correlations of baseline SUPPS-P scores with these external variables measured up to 12 months later supported predictive validity.
Internal consistency was generally acceptable across subscales and moderate intraclass correlation coefficients supported acceptable test-retest reliability.
Though the results presented here support the five-factor structure of the SUPPS-P, attention to the performance of the lack of perseverance scale in this sample is warranted.

Specifically, lack of perseverance had the weakest item-total correlations, several weak factor loadings, the weakest relationships with external validators (and did not correlate with internalizing symptoms, as it does in a vast majority of validation studies) [13, 18, 21, 26, 27], and the lowest internal consistency and test-retest reliability.

text.text: This pattern is notable as, by many established thresholds, the lack of perseverance subscale performed at or below borderline acceptability in present sample.

There is some evidence that the performance of this subscale can be worse in adolescents [57], which is likely attributable to executive functioning, cognitive control, and capacity for sustained attention still being in development during this stage [58] [59] [60], but a handful of other studies of SUPPS-P translations have shown that the lack of perseverance subscale also performed more poorly than the others in young adult and adult samples [13, 31].

text.text: Given that the present study was conducted in a sample of students, the non-student nature of the Swedish sample cannot explain the relatively poor performance of the lack of perseverance subscale.

It is notable that one of the few other validation studies of a SUPPS-P translation that observed low reliability for the lack of perseverance subscale is that in another Scandinavian sample, and that this study was also the only other to find no association between lack of perseverance and internalizing symptoms [31].

text.text: This may suggest that there is a broader cultural influence impacting how lack of perseverance manifests in Scandinavian populations and/or how these items are interpreted and understood in this cultural context.

The SUPPS-P items capturing lack of perseverance focus on emotional discomfort with incomplete tasks (e.g., "unfinished tasks really bother me") and behavioral persistence toward task completion (e.g., "I finish what I start"); notably, the two emotion-based items evidenced weak loadings (λ=0.252-0.490), while the behavior-based items performed well (λ=0.657-0.859).

In a culture that places strong emphasis on work-life balance, and in which it is generally acceptable to leave a task unfinished in favor of maintaining such balance and personal well-being [61], aversive emotional experiences related to incomplete tasks may be less common and less relevant to capturing (lack of) perseverance than more behaviorally-oriented indicators.

The "I would like to learn to fly an airplane" item has been shown to perform poorly in adolescents, attributed to learning to fly an airplane potentially being of less interest to youth than it was when these items were originally developed [57].

text.text: In line with this, the factor loading for the other activity-based SUPPS-P item ("I would enjoy the sensation of skiing very fast down a high mountain slope") was only slightly stronger than that for the "I would like to learn to fly an airplane" item (λ=0.550 vs. λ=0.452) and was substantially weaker than the loading for the "I quite enjoy taking risks" item (λ=0.795).

The item "I welcome new and exciting experiences and sensations, even if they are a little frightening and unconventional" (λ=0.486) performs well in adolescent samples when the phrasing has been modified to be more developmentally appropriate ("I like new, thrilling things, even if they are a little scary") [9, 57], but similarly performs poorly compared to other items when the phrasing of the original SUPPS-P is retained [23].

text.text: However, given that the loadings for these items were borderline acceptable by some recommended thresholds [56], it is arguable whether the scale should be modified from the existing version that is widely used and very well-established.

text.text: However, development of an updated version with examples more relevant to contemporary society coupled with modified phrasing more appropriate for adolescents may be viable ways to address these potential shortcomings.

Further studies in novel samples will be required to determine if the patterns observed here are idiosyncratic to these data, or if these particular items require modification to more precisely measure sensation seeking in Danish adolescents.
These findings should be interpreted in light of limitations.
First, this sample was drawn from a high school-based study.
As such, students who dropped out or opted to attend vocational school are not captured here.

Second, although a member of the study team was present for all survey administrations, it is possible that the classroom environment in which the survey was administered impacted how students responded to the survey.
Third, phrasing from the adult SUPPS-P was retained, which may have impacted the performance of some items in this adolescent sample, as described above.
Finally, measures within the survey were not randomized, such that positioning of the SUPPS-P within the larger survey may have impacted how students responded to questionnaire.
This study presents initial validation of the Danish version of the Short UPPS-P Impulsive Behavior Scale [8], supporting its suitabililty for assessing impulsivity in adolescents.

text.text: Although the best-fit model identified here was consistent with a large literature supporting a five-factor solution and the SUPPS-P showed acceptable validity and reliability by several metrics, results also indicated that this measure could be further optimized to capture impulsivity in Scandinavian adolescents.

Integrating cultural considerations and modifying the language of some items in the Danish SUPPS-P to be more developmentally appropriate for the adolescent age group are two viable avenues to futher improve the performance of this measure.
